units.text: MultiTEA: A model-driven framework for the co-design and automatic generation of applications for ASD users
Introduction

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurological dysfunction of genetic origin that persists over time and appears early in life, causing symptoms that affect communication, social interaction, and flexibility in behavior and thought [1].It is one of the most common neurological disorders among young people, and its diagnosis has significantly increased in recent decades.The World Health Organization reports that 1 in 100 children worldwide has ASD, although prevalence rates vary by country. 1  ASD presents a wide range of manifestations, hence why it is referred to as a spectrum [2].Due to the heterogeneity of this condition, no two individuals with ASD are alike, and symptoms can vary based on the level of involvement and severity [3].This variability can be influenced by several factors, such as the support the individual receives, the presence of other associated disorders or illnesses, like psychiatric disorders or intellectual disability, and the level of language development [4,5].As a result, it is important to approach the disorder in a patient-specific manner and provide tailored support that considers their unique abilities and circumstances [6,7].

New information and communication technologies (ICT) can offer support to people with ASD and their families, promoting their autonomy [8], self-management [9], and social integration [10], in different contexts, such as work [11,12] or school [13].These assistive technologies can provide personalized support tailored to each individual's communication needs, sensory difficulties, preferences, and interests, while offering a motivating and highly predictable environment [14].Many technological developments and applications have been created for ASD users, especially with mobile and touch support, which have proven their effectiveness in interventions and skills training [15,16].

In recent years, some proposals in the form of guidelines for the development of software solutions aimed at ASD users have emerged, there are hardly any methodological approaches or frameworks to assist developers in the design and implementation of these applications.Consequently, it is essential to advance in this area by proposing a framework to assist developers in this endeavor.

The aim of this paper is to describe such framework proposal, called MultiTEA, which follows the MDD approach and supports several stages of design and co-design.The application of this framework will result in multi-device touch applications for the training of social skills (planning, anticipation, communication, and emotion recognition) by users with ASD.For this purpose, the authors of this work have previous experience in the development of applications for ASD users [17] and in the automatic generation, following the MDD approach, of single-user and collaborative applications [18].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.Section 2 reviews some works related to the use of new technologies for people with ASD, as well as some of the most relevant proposals for the design, implementation, and evaluation of this type of application.Section 3 briefly describes the previous experience of the authors of this paper in the development of mobile and touch applications for ASD users and in collaborative application development following an MDD approach, ending with the list of requirements of the proposed framework (MultiTEA).This framework is described in detail in Sectsion 4 and 5, and in Section 6, the results of a preliminary evaluation of the framework with therapists are presented.Finally, in Section 7, conclusions are included and some lines of continuation of this research are presented.
Related works

This section describes the status related to the use of new technologies for people with ASD, as well as the existing proposals to support the design, implementation, and evaluation of applications oriented to this group of users.
ICT and ASD

Currently, there is a growing interest in providing technological support to users with ASD [19].New technologies are well accepted by this collective, which feels motivated and comfortable in the highly predictable environment that the applications offer [20].These applications focus on offering support in the areas most affected in this type of user, such as communication [21], socialization [10,22,23], behavioral and cognitive flexibility [24,25], need for anticipation [17,25], emotion recognition [26,27], self-management [9], or the control of certain emotional states, such as anxiety and stress [28].

Most of these applications have been developed for mobile devices [15,16,29,30], such as smartphones and tablets [31,32], as well as other advanced touch devices, such as multitouch tabletops [33][34][35][36][37].Among the developments carried out, the use of serious games for communicative and social skills learning and training highlights [21] [28,38,39], mainly aimed at children or high-functioning ASD users [40].New interaction paradigms have also been exploited, such as the recreation of artificial scenarios in Virtual Reality [41] and Augmented Reality [21,42] applications, as well as in the context of Metaverse [43].These applications provide sensory information, mainly visual, auditory, and haptic information, which can be used to simulate activities, allowing interaction with the virtual environment.Most recently, the use of socially assistive robots (SARs) in interventions with people with ASD to work on emotional regulation and empathy [44,45], as well as the integration of mobile solutions with wearable devices [46,47], has gained interest.Proposals are also being presented in the field of the Internet of Things (IoT) and smart environments, to improve support for users with ASD in different environments (workspace, school, and home) [48,49].

Many of these developments have been evaluated and have proven to be effective in enhancing and training the communication and social skills of individuals with ASD [15,24,50], and all of them pursue, as a last resort, to improve the inclusion and quality of life of individuals with ASD and their families [8].
Development of applications for users with ASD

Most of the developments aimed at people with ASD have been created ad hoc and following a designer-driven approach, without guidelines or frameworks to assist designers and developers during the creation process.Recently, new approaches have been proposed for the development of applications specifically oriented to ASD users that are more guided and structured, i.e., based on sequences of stages or development cycles that incorporate design recommendations and guidelines, as well as evaluation methods and instruments.

The field in which the most contributions have been made is the design of serious games for people with autism.Thus, in [51,52], a framework and a set of guidelines for the design of serious games in the field of special education, specifically, oriented to users with intellectual disabilities and ASD, are proposed.These authors identify a set of elements to be considered when creating this type of software and advocate the adoption of a participatory design approach as a core element of the process.In [53] a gamification design method for applications to improve social skills in ASD users is presented, consisting of three phases: analysis, design & development, and evaluation.In the analysis phase, the involvement of therapists, parents, and children with ASD is suggested.In the second phase, it is defined and identified the gamification elements and mechanisms to be incorporated in the final software product (which can be web, mobile or a virtual, augmented, or mixed reality development).Finally, in the evaluation phase, it is planned to measure motivation, engagement, and effectiveness-interaction skills.In [54] a framework for the design of games and other assistive technologies in the field of emotion teaching for children with ASD is described.To this end, the authors identify six design elements or factors to consider in this type of games (matching, recognizing, observing, understanding, generalizing, and mimicking), based on the integration of two theoretical models: Kolb's experiential learning model and Piaget's cognitive development model.In [55] the authors describe an iterative-incremental design process, based on prototypes, for the creation of a serious game of the Escape Room type, and establish a series of guidelines.These authors advocate the need to involve children with ASD and their therapists in the game design and refinement process.In [56] the authors present and evaluate a serious game development framework (SGDF) for teaching vocabulary to children with ASD, proposing a set of components and design patterns related to the structure of the game.In [57] authors describe an inclusive design approach to develop therapeutic games, which promotes the integration of the expertise of mental health specialists, the child with ASD and design experts in the game creation process.In this work, strategies for eliciting requirements and a method for their integration and orchestration in the development process are provided.

Other works focus on proposing methods and techniques to be used in specific phases of the development process of the application for ASD users.For example, in [58] it is described how a requirements analysis technique from the Human-Computer Interaction, such as "Personas and Scenarios" [59] should be applied in the analysis and co-design phases of this type of software.There are also several proposals of guidelines to be used in the design phase, highlighting the AutismGuide usability guidelines [60], consisting of a set of 69 recommendations, obtained from a literature review, to be taken into account when developing software solutions adapted to ASD users.Design recommendations for specific environments and interaction paradigms have also been proposed.Thus, [61] compiles, from a literature review, some design considerations and guidelines for creating Virtual Reality applications for the ASD community.In [62] a set of usability guidelines for the interface design of mobile applications for autism is proposed.On the other hand, [63] compiles, following an exploratory analysis of the literature, a total of 28 guidelines, distributed in 10 categories, to be considered in the design of accessible websites for users with ASD.

Methods have also been proposed to be applied for accessibility and usability evaluation of these applications, highlighting the methodological approach described in [64], which includes nine factors to improve the User Experience (UX) in interactive applications for ASD users (engaging, predictable, structured, interactive, generalizable, customizable, sense-aware, attention-retaining, and frustration-free) [65].These authors have also created an evaluation instrument, a checklist, for the assessment of compliance with the UX design guidelines they propose [66], which has a full version (consisting of 9 categories and 50 items) and a compact version (with 9 categories and 24 items).On the other hand, in [67] an evidence-based evaluation method to assess the effectiveness of digital support for ASD users is presented.To this end, they propose to collect evidence from autistic people themselves, their families, as well as from professionals and researchers related to autism.This framework suggests obtaining evidence to measure three aspects (reliability, engagement, and effectiveness of the technology) and that such evidence be obtained from three sources of information: hands-on experience, academic sources, expert views, and online reviews.

Regarding the implementation phase, it is worth mentioning the FRIDA framework [68].It proposes an agile development method for accessible software for ASD users, based on components or building blocks, which allows the creation and adaptation of apps to train social and emotional skills.FRIDA authors also provide a set of design recommendations [69] and evaluation heuristics for this type of applications [70].As for the MDD approach, there is only one proposal [71,72] which supports the generation of adaptive scenarios in mobile learning games for children with ASD.It consists of a skill-driven adaptivity process based on the specification or modeling of the game, the child's profile, and the scenario (objective, structural, and features scenarios), supporting the generation of different levels of difficulty in the game obtained by applying the method.

In short, there is a growing trend to adopt more participatory developments in which experts and end-users are more deeply involved.Moreover, software applications should be accepted, engaging, and usable for ASD users while being effective in terms of assistive and therapeutic goals.To that end, it is necessary the participation of therapists and families during software design since they are the ones who know the needs of the potential final ASD users.
Previous work and proposal requirements

This section describes the fundamentals of the MultiTEA proposal, based on the previous contributions of the authors of this article to the development of software for people with ASD (the PlanTEA application) and to model-driven development for the generation of collaborative applications (the Learn-CIAM framework).Finally, the MultiTEA requirements are established, derived from the lessons learned during the previous work carried out.
PlanTEA

PlanTEA [17] is a mobile application aimed at children with ASD, aged 4-10 years, to help plan and anticipate medical appointments.It was created on Android and to be used mainly on tablet-type touch devices.This application supports two roles: the planner role and the child role.The planner role, which can be played by family members or caregivers, is responsible for designing the planning of visits and medical examinations, while the user with the child role can review and monitor the planning while the visit to the medical center is taking place (Fig. 1).The application includes a reward system to motivate children to complete and track tasks, as well as stress and waiting time management mechanisms.In addition, PlanTEA includes a communication notebook to facilitate the exchange of information with medical staff.

PlanTEA supports alternative and augmentative communication mechanisms,2 so that its main functionalities (planning and communication notebook) are based on the use of visual representations (pictograms).Even so, it includes customization mechanisms since it gives the option of using real images and photographs in the planning.In contrast to most of the existing developments in the literature, the design process of PlanTEA follows specific design guidelines (AutismGuide) for this group of users [73], with the ultimate goal of improving the usability of the developed application.

The development and evaluation of the PlanTEA application were carried out in collaboration with the AUTRADE association. 3 During its design, and as stated by experts and family members in the evaluation, the need for a tool that would allow the collaborative participation of all stakeholders was detected.This necessity motivated the creation of the MultiTEA proposal.
Learn-CIAM and SpacEclipse

Learn-CIAM [18] is a proposal, framed in the paradigm of MDD, that allows the design and semi-automatic generation of collaborative applications.Specifically, it allows the generation of textual and graphical editors, as well as multi-user browsers.In this framework, we focus on its capacity to generate multi-domain graphical editors, since ASD users will mainly make use of graphical representations (typically pictograms).

Learn-CIAM consists of two phases: a first phase, which supports the generation of domain-independent graphical editors, i.e., the creation of diagrams based on a set of nodes and links; and a second phase, which incorporates components and widgets necessary in any collaborative system (communication, coordination, and awareness4 mechanisms), thanks to the use of a previous framework (SpaceEclipse) [74] [75].

The result obtained (once the characteristics of the graphic models to be created have been defined) is a collaborative graphic editor equipped with a palette of elements (nodes and links) as well as a shared editing area or canvas.This tool can be enriched by multiuser task support components, such as a chat, a session panel, and telepointers, as well as voting and turn-taking components [76].Therefore, the Learn-CIAM framework has enormous potential for the generation of applications oriented to people with ASD, such as PlanTEA.In this context, the creation of the MultiTEA framework helps to fill the gap in support for the design and implementation of applications for people with ASD.
Proposal requirements
The MultiTEA framework should support certain characteristics, as discussed below:

• Activities based on visual supports.Visual supports are aids for learning and communicative interaction that facilitate the performance of daily routine activities by a person with ASD [77].To that end, the use of pictorial representations (pictograms) helps ASD people to communicate, understand social situations, reduce anxiety, plan, complete, and anticipate tasks, and therefore promote independence [78].Then, pictograms should play an essential role in the design of the activities to be supported.• Participatory design and customized activities.There is agreement that the participation of people with ASD and their families in the design and evaluation process positively influences the adaptation of technology to their needs [79].In the case of ASD users with significant communication problems or high support needs, it is necessary to involve family members and therapists, who are the ones who best know the needs, abilities, and preferences of the ASD user, being essential to customize and adapt activities and contents [80,81].Some of the features that can be jointly determined include the type and difficulty of the activities, the most appropriate and effective rewards, or the format of the visual aids to be used, among other aspects.For example, caregivers and other professionals should evaluate and decide which type of visual representation (real objects, photographs, line drawings, words, or combinations of these visual representations) is most appropriate for each individual with ASD, depending on their individual needs, preferences, and interests [82].Once the type of visual support has been selected, it can be used in planners, calendars, augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) notebooks, to-do lists, etc., which they use in their daily lives [83].Therefore, the proposed framework includes participatory design features that involve the main stakeholders, who will act as collaborators and co-designers of the final software product.

• Model-Driven Development approach.The proposed design and development process will follow a Model-Driven Development (MDD) approach and will allow the semi-automatic generation of the final software application [84].This process will follow different stages of creation, refinement, and customization of the activities, resulting in intermediate prototypes (or activity templates) that can be modified and customized in the collaborative stages of review and co-design.Following an MDD approach will also allow for the incorporation of accessibility and usability guideline checks during the software development process [62].• Generative Participatory Design Methodology (GPDM).The proposed framework will allow the adoption of this methodology [85].The GPDM is an approach within participatory design that focuses on harnessing the creativity and lived experiences of users through the use of generative tools and techniques.This methodology emphasizes the co-creation of future innovations, and among its key aspects are the collaboration between designers and non-designers in co-design sessions.Its application proposes the use of generative tools in which tangible artifacts are created, which are subjected to iterative processes of analysis, evaluation, and refinement.The insights gathered from the generative participatory sessions are integrated into the design process, influencing decisions on features, functionality, and aesthetics.The GPDM can be very effective in the development of software for users with ASD.Since people with ASD have a wide range of needs, generative tools can be customized to be accessible and relevant to each individual.Through the co-creation sessions, users can express their preferences using tangible tools and visual methods, which help designers understand their needs.

The iterative process involves refinement of the prototypes, in which the interface is adjusted (visualized elements, colors, and fonts, among others), ensuring that software is more accessible, usable, and tailored to the unique routines and preferences of users with ASD.This process results in systems that are more inclusive, empowering, and closely aligned with the daily experiences and preferences of users.

• Multi-device.The framework will support the automatic generation of cross-platform applications, mainly based on touch interaction styles, that can be deployed on different devices (tablets, multitouch tabletops).
MultiTEA
This section describes the main features of the MultiTEA proposal, the stages it supports, and the technologies used for its development.
Activities supported

MultiTEA supports the design and semi-automatic generation of applications to perform different types of activities aimed at improving the social skills of people with ASD.So far, MultiTEA supports two types of activities:

1) Planning and anticipation of activities defined by sequences of steps graphically represented, as well as design and consulting routines.2) Emotion recognition.To do so, the user can select, among a set of options (pictograms or images), which one represents a certain emotion.
Specification of activities

The supported activities can be specified by a generic graphical notation, which allows the creation of activity templates.This template will be composed mainly of nodes, links, and annotations on links.

When designing planning activities, the nodes (generic pictograms) represent people, places, and actions (Table 1) and the links specify the order of the nodes that compose the sequence of pictograms (Fig. 2.1).Both nodes and links may include annotations, i.e., aspects to be considered during planning, related to time management, interpersonal communication, or the possibility of including incentives.The types of annotations supported are:

1) Social stories.The proposed notation gives the possibility to include directives or phrases to be used in social interaction situations, the so-called social stories (Fig. 2.a), which were devised as a tool to help people with ASD to better understand the nuances of interpersonal communication and thus interact in a more effective and appropriate way [86].Social stories are short, simple, and should be highly personalized [87].Their use has been shown to be effective in a variety of contexts and helps individuals with ASD to understand the most relevant social cues, the others' perspective, and to make an appropriate response in each situation [88].
2) Alternative and augmentative communication (ACC) notebook. The graphic notation

allows for the specification of the steps in which it may be necessary to make use of the ACC notebook.3) Temporal information (deadlines, waiting times, schedules, appointments, etc.) (Fig. 2.b).Time management and waiting times are challenges for people with ASD [89].Thus, knowing the exact time of appointments and being aware of the time passing by timers or countdown clocks help them manage their anxiety.4) Rewards, incentives, or positive reinforcement elements at certain points in the schedule are contemplated in the notation, aiming to improve the user's motivation and engagement in following the plan [90].5) Calming activity or object (Fig. 2.c).Often, people with ASD need to carry objects (for example, a soothing toy, a garment, or a book) with certain sensory characteristics, which allow them to calm down and self-regulate in stressful times [90].On the other hand, certain entertainment activities help them to better cope with some anxious situations, especially during waiting times.

Regarding emotion recognition (Table 1), a node has been included to specify the scene or face whose emotion must be recognized (target emotion) (Fig. 2.d); other node to indicate the response options (Fig. 2.e), and two types of links to connect the response options with the solution, indicating whether the connection (response given) is correct or not.These links are enriched with the specification, by the designer of the activity, of the positive and negative feedback to be emitted depending on the selection made by the user.
Method proposed
The proposed framework (MultiTEA) consists of three stages:
Stage 1: Preliminary design

First, the activity to be performed by the ASD user (Fig. 3.1) is designed by the therapist or ASD specialist, producing as a result a generic activity template (Fig. 2).To support the individual design stage of the activity template, the graphical specification technique or Fig. 3 Stages of application of the framework for obtaining multiplatform applications for users with ASD notation presented in Section 4.2 is used.For this purpose, a palette is available to create the design of the activity in the drawing area or canvas by dragging and dropping graphic elements (nodes, links, and annotations on links).
Stage 2: Co-design stage

Once the activity template (planning or emotion recognition) has been created, the next stage is the personalization of the activity, in which the therapist and family members or caregivers will be involved (Fig. 3.2).This collaborative phase, with distributed support, takes as input the activity template obtained in the previous phase.Then, components (nodes or links) can be added or removed, and other aspects related to the nodes can be specified.For example, whether the nodes will use figurative pictograms or real images, or whether they will name specific places, people, or sites well-known to the ASD user.Annotations can also be specified, such as the selection of calming activities and objects or rewards and awards of value to the end user.Likewise, the sentences or phrases that will make up the social stories can be incorporated (Fig. 4).During this phase, the participation of family members or caregivers is essential, as they are the ones who best know the preferences and particularities of the user with ASD.

This stage can be performed either in a co-localized way with a single activity editor instance or synchronously and distributed across multiple instances.The COVID-19 pandemic emphasized the need for distributed work in different fields, such as education [91] or health [92], which this framework supports.
Stage 3: Use of the generated application

Once the design of the activity has been customized and agreed upon by family members and therapists, the final version of the software is obtained, which can be deployed on  6 Users interacting with the application instances generated for several touch devices various devices (Fig. 6).In this last stage, the users of the application will be able to work autonomously, for example, by visualizing and thus anticipating the steps included in a plan or performing emotion recognition activities.For this purpose, they can use the applications on their desktops, laptops, or tablets.The generated application can also be used in collocated collaboration contexts, using a larger display device and multitouch support (an interactive whiteboard or tabletop), or in synchronous distributed collaboration scenarios, in which they will make use of identifying avatars, color codes, telepointers, and communication via audio and chat (Fig. 3.3).
Technological support of the proposal

This section describes the technological support of the MultiTEA proposal (Fig. 7), including an overview of the technologies and programming languages used (Table 2) and describing the development process (Fig. 8) and the architecture of the framework created (Fig. 9).

Figure 8 describes the technological process involved in the development of MultiTEA, indicating the main components involved in Fig. 7 and the flow between them.Next, each of the implemented and necessary files in each of the phases that make up the generation process are described: 1) the specification and generation of the single-user graphical editor; 2) the addition of collaborative functionality to the editor; and 3) the automatic transformation and generation of ASD multitouch and multidevice tools.

In the first stage, Eclipse Epsilon is used.Epsilon is a MDD framework that provides a set of languages and tools to facilitate MDD processes.It includes several domain-specific languages (DSLs), such as model transformation, code generation, model merging and model validation.By providing a set of standardized languages and tools, the Epsilon framework helps to simplify the process of developing and maintaining complex MDD frameworks.In this approach, Epsilon is necessary to create and semiautomatically generate the single-user graphical editor for designing activities for planning and training in emotion recognition (ASD diagrams).With this aim, three different files have been created: a) the meta-model, in Emfatic language, for the description of the entities and relationships of the graphical editor (.emf file), and launching the automatic generation process; b) the customization file, in EOL (Epsilon Object Language), for ordering the elements of the palette and customizing the visual aspect of nodes and links (.eol file); and c) the validation file, written in EVL (Epsilon Validation Language), for including the restrictions and constraints that must be incorporated in the meta-model and, therefore, into the final graphical editor (.evl file) (Fig. 7.1).Once all of them are ready, Epsilon can initiate an automatic generation process, thus obtaining the final single-user graphical editor (Figs. 8 and 9.a).This is the main component, providing a therapist the possibility to model an ASD diagram (Fig. 3.1).

Once the graphical editor has been created, a collaborative version of it can be instantiated by adding collaborative features from the SpacEclipse [74] [75] plugin (Fig. 7.2).SpacEclipse incorporates a variety of notable features, including the incorporation of several collaboration widgets such as chat, a turn-taking panel and a session panel.Moreover, it is equipped with effective awareness support through color differentiation for each user, semaphores and sound notifications for user interface changes.This plugin, in turn, relies on the Eclipse Communication Framework (ECF).ECF is an open-source communication middleware that provides a flexible and extensible framework for developing distributed applications and is essential for ensuring the proper functioning of the SpacEclipse plugin.When both the graphical editor and SpacEclipse are available in the same Eclipse workspace, the next step involves combining them using a patch (CollaborativeDiagram.patch) (Fig. 8).This patch is responsible for the integration of the graphical editor and the SpacEclipse plugin, just modifying the main SpacEclipse class (Fig. 9.b).Specifically, the 'Space' Java class, designed to integrate any generic DSL Graphical Editor, such as the ASD diagram, with the SpacEclipse plugin.Furthermore, it is also important to note that the 'SpaceClient' class was implemented to integrate the SpacEclipse plugin with any ECF Generic Server, thus enabling collaborative functionality (Fig. 9.c).Naturally, in any collaborative session, both therapists and families/caregivers can launch and automate the generation process of multitouch and multidevice tools (Fig. 3.2).

In the third stage, the semiautomatic generation of multitouch and multidevice tools takes place (Fig. 7.3).The final code of the cross-platform application is generated in GoJS,  a JavaScript framework for building interactive diagrams and graphical representations of data in web applications.With GoJS, developers can easily create complex, interactive diagrams that respond to user interactions, support drag-and-drop, zooming, and scrolling, and can be easily integrated into any web application.Overall, GoJS is a powerful and flexible framework for building interactive diagrams and visualizations in web applications.It is also worth noting the addition of collaboration features to the final tools.For this purpose, two complementary technologies are used, namely TogetherJS and Glitch.TogetherJS is an open-source tool developed by Mozilla that provides a solution for real-time collaboration in web applications.It allows users to collaborate in real-time on the same web page, share screens, and share control of the keyboard and mouse to facilitate collaboration in web development.Whilst Glitch is a cloud-based web development platform that provides an easy-to-use interface for creating and hosting web applications.Using Glitch, developers can quickly create and publish web applications without the need for complex setup or configuration, making it an ideal platform for both beginners and experienced developers alike.

The process of automatically generating final applications entails employing the Epsilon framework in conjunction with previously established GoJS code (for individual work) or combining Eclipse Epsilon with GoJS, Together JS, and Glitch (for collaborative efforts).To this end, three templates have been developed using Epsilon technology.Specifically, three templates in the EGL are essential (Fig. 8): a) the rules.egxtemplate, responsible Concerning the integration of collaborative capabilities, the same templates are employed to determine whether the ASD diagram designates collaborative work.If confirmed, the templates proceed automatically to include references for both TogetherJS (the URI of the framework) and Glitch (where the server is located) in the 'index.html'file.Additionally, the necessary collaborative features are appended to the 'teaw.js'file (Fig. 9.d).Thus, by leveraging both TogetherJS and Glitch, collaborative functionality is integrated into the generated final web tools.This combination has made it feasible to develop web-based applications that facilitate real-time collaboration between users, which can be deployed on different devices (mobiles, tablets, and interactive whiteboards/tabletops) (Fig. 3.3).
Activity design validation

In the individual and collaborative design phases (stages 1 and 2), mechanisms for checking, validating, and correcting the activity designs created have been incorporated.Thanks to the use of EVL technology, it has been possible to specify constraints to be met by the activity model.These may be structural or related to the syntax of the specification.For example, Fig. 10.a shows an example of this type of constraint, which indicates that in an emotion recognition activity, the link to the correct solution should be of the positive type.The editor will also generate a warning or error if two nodes in a plan have not been linked or if any property (for example, the description of a node) has not been specified.Also, it is possible to limit the number of pictograms to be included in a plan, so that the editor will warn if this number is exceeded (Fig. 10.b).Some of these errors and warnings may be corrected manually by the user, and others may be auto-fixed automatically by the tool.Figure 10.c shows an example of this type of constraint, which removes duplicate positive-type links in an emotion recognition activity.Some of these verifications are necessary to support the automatic generation of the final tool as, for example, those related to the order of the nodes in the activities.

In addition to these restrictions, validations related to the usability and accessibility of the final application have been included, based on the checklist for the evaluation of the UX of people with ASD proposed by [66].Some examples are:

• "The system provides rewards to the user for positive actions or good performance".The fulfillment of this guideline implies, for example, that in the activities of the planning type, it is mandatory to incorporate a node of the award or recompense type (Fig. 10.d).• "The system delivers constant feedback to the user in a clear and concise manner.This must be not only through text but also through visual elements or audio".In the case of activities for emotion recognition training, it will be mandatory to specify the type of feedback, both positive and negative, in the links of the model.• "The system uses a clear, familiar, precise and appropriate language".The co-editing phase allows participants in the design process to customize the activity and adapt it to the particularities of the final users.This guideline reminds them that, if they see fit, it could be appropriate to include familiar images and texts for the ASD user in the design of the activities.
Preliminary evaluation

A preliminary evaluation of MultiTEA's usefulness, acceptance, and intention to be used by psychologists and therapists specializing in ASD was carried out.This evaluation was also intended to identify possible shortcomings and opportunities for improvement.
Evaluation design and instruments

As a preliminary evaluation, a descriptive study was designed, based on the use of a subjective perception questionnaire in which psychologists and therapists were involved.Participants were recruited from various local, regional, and national associations and institutions working with people with autism.To do so, an e-mail was sent to the contact addresses of the technical departments of these associations.Specifically, contact was made with the Association of People Affected by Autism and Other Developmental Disorders (AUTRADE5 ), of local scope, the regional Autism Federation of Castilla-La Mancha (FACLM 6 ) and the Spanish Autism Federation (FESPAU 7 ), with which our university and research group have active collaboration and transfer agreements.

The experts who agreed to participate received an e-mail with a link to a form deployed in MS Forms, 8 which included the informed consent.This indicated the purpose of the study and what it consisted of, informed of the voluntariness of participation and the possibility of withdrawing at any time, gave details related to confidentiality and data processing, and, finally, provided contact information.Once they agreed to participate, they could access a 5-min demonstration video 9 describing the framework, the different stages, and examples of use of the tools to be used in each of them.The experts could watch the video as many times as they considered necessary.Once they had watched the video and considered that they had understood the proposal, they could answer a questionnaire consisting of a series of items in Likert format with 5 response options (1: "strongly disagree" and 5: "strongly agree") grouped into different categories, which were intended to measure the following aspects:

• Therapist's previous experience (TPE).The first set of questions asked about the therapist's previous experience with ASD (TPE1), as well as in the use of software applications or technologies aimed at users of this collective (TPE2).
• Usefulness and need of the main stages and aspects of the MultiTEA framework (NEU).
A series of Likert scales were included to rate the need or utility of each of the stages of the proposal.
• Innovativeness of the proposal and some of the aspects it supports (INN). A series of

Likert scales were included so that therapists could rate the degree of innovativeness of some of the features of the developed framework.• TAM-based questionnaire.This block included six items based on and adapted from the TAM framework (Technology Acceptance Model) [93] which measures aspects related to the ease of use (PEU), usefulness (PU), and intention to use (ITU) the Multi-TEA proposal.• Open-ended questions.
A series of open-ended questions were included to allow respondents to indicate the strengths and weaknesses of the proposal, as well as any other comments or suggestions for improvement.
Participants

The measurement instrument was filled out by a total of 21 participants (18 women and 3 men).Of them, 16 were therapists, 10 of whom had previous experience with people with ASD.The remaining participants were psychologists, social workers, educators, or support personnel with experience with ASD.
Results

Table 3 shows the descriptive statistics (mean, median, and mode), as well as the percentages of responses to the different items used in this evaluation.The statistics were calculated using the SPSS statistical package.The answers given by the participants to the items of the questionnaire and to the open-ended questions can be consulted in Appendix 1 (Tables 4 and 5, respectively).With respect to the usefulness of the main features of the proposal, the most highly rated aspects are the possibility of accessing the activities through different devices  Regarding the assessment of the items related to the acceptance and adoption of this framework (Table 3 and Fig. 11), the respondents considered the proposed tools to be easy to use, although more so for experts (m = 4.48, sd = 0.98) than for family members.They also rated very positively the usefulness of MultiTEA for the design of activities, especially valuing the possibility of customization (m = 4.57, sd = 0.87).They also stated that if the tools were at their disposal, they would use them and would also recommend their use to other professionals.

Finally, the answers given to the open-ended questions were compiled (Table 5 in Appendix 1).The aspects pointed out by the respondents as strengths and weaknesses of the proposal as well as the frequency of responses related to these issues can be seen in Fig. 12.According to them, most of the respondents valued positively the possibility of adapting and customizing activities to the ASD user (43%10 ), the deployment in various scenarios and devices (29%), and the involvement of several stakeholders in the collaborative process of designing and refining the activities (19%), mainly the inclusion of families Fig. 11 Graph of average scores of the TAM framework items, of acceptance and adoption of the proposal (ease of use, usefulness, and intention to use) in this process (24%).Ease of use was also pointed out as one of the features to be highlighted in the proposal (19%).In general, the main concerns of the participants were related to the need for training to use the tools (43%), access to the technological resources (29%), as well as the intervention of an expert in stage 1 (24%).In this sense, some of the respondents pointed out the possibility of following the process without going through stage 1, i.e., that family members could lead the whole process of designing the activities.

As for the suggestions for improvement made by the respondents, the possibility of using various formats in the activities (pictograms only, pictograms and text, and text only) is proposed to better adapt to the different abstraction levels and communicative needs of the users.Again, in this section they insist on some aspects indicated as limitations or weaknesses, such as the need for training, which can be partly solved by creating resources to support it, such as manuals or video tutorials, as well as the possibility of dispensing with the expert in the first phase of the proposed process.The convenience of integrating the proposed tools with others used by this group of users, such as Augmentative or Alternative Communication (AAC) systems, or the coding of pictogram types or categories by colors are also pointed out as improvements to be considered.Finally, they also comment on the need to modify, in stage 3 and in the particular case of planning, the representation generated, in order to deal with changes and unexpected events.
Discussion and proposals for improvement

The initial aim of this work was to assess the feasibility of applying an MDD approach to obtain applications for people with ASD, which would help developers in the design and implementation of this type of software system.We consider that this objective has been achieved by proposing a framework composed of a series of stages that support the automatic generation of this type of application.

The preliminary evaluation of the proposal has produced very positive results and proposals for improvement that will be addressed in the future.The most highly valued aspects were the customization of activities to the preferences and characteristics of ASD users, as well as the possibility of multi-device deployment.More personalized support, tailored to the needs, difficulties, preferences and interests of each individual, is essential to provide a motivating and engaging environment [94].For its part, cross-device deployment, especially to mobile and touch support, has proven its effectiveness in interventions and skills training [15,16].In addition, being able to deploy the activities to be performed on tabletop and multi-touch board devices will allow their use in collaborative and educational contexts [38,95].

Another of the most valued features of the proposal has been the incorporation of the collaborative design stage.In this sense, the benefits of applying this co-design approach, both with ASD users and their families, have been demonstrated in several works [96][97][98][99].This approach has been shown to improve the motivation, engagement, and adoption of software developed by end-users [100].Family members and therapists are the ones who best know the needs, abilities and preferences of the user with ASD, being essential to customize and adapt activities and content [20,21].Family members and therapists bring different perspectives and knowledge to the design process, which are complementary and enrich the final result [22].Collaboration between family members and therapists during the design process makes the final product better adapted to the needs of users with ASD, making it more usable and accessible.

The unique and original contribution of this work is the proposal of a method for the design and automatic generation of cross-platform applications oriented to ASD users, following a model-driven approach and a generative participatory design methodology.Despite the existence of works that address the design of systems aimed at this user collective (Section 2.2), which are based on guidelines, checklists, and methods or sets of stages to be followed in the design of this type of system, there were no proposals that followed the MDD approach.In addition, among the benefits of applying the GPDM are the creation of more user-centered solutions and the obtaining of richer insights.Since the design is co-created with users, the final outcomes are more likely to be aligned with their real needs and desires, leading to higher user satisfaction and product adoption.In addition, by allowing users to generate artifacts that capture their experiences, designers can uncover nuanced insights that are not easily obtained through other methods [85].

However, the results of the preliminary assessment suggest that there are some aspects to be improved, which are discussed below.One of the main issues to be addressed when creating applications for users with ASD is the great diversity of features presented by individuals in this collective.No two people with ASD are alike, which is why there is talk of the existence of a spectrum with an enormous heterogeneity of particular characteristics [2].

Therefore, designing software for individuals with ASD requires careful consideration of their diverse needs and varying degrees of severity [101,102].Key aspects to consider in this regard include interface customization and flexibility to adapt to different cognitive abilities, communication styles, and sensory sensitivities of users.This can be achieved through configurations that allow adjusting the level of complexity and type of interactions, as well as the ability to customize the interface (text size, colors, symbols).In this sense, the described framework is considered applicable to a wide range of ASD users, as it considers the particular characteristics, needs, and preferences that are reported by family members and caregivers in the initial stages (stages 1 and 2), thus supporting a certain degree of customization of the contents to be displayed.

In this type of system, the interface must be simple and predictable, allowing visual, auditory and tactile stimuli to be adjusted to prevent sensory overload [65,66].MultiTEA is considered to generate visually simple applications that minimize the excess of visual information on the screen, thus avoiding the sensory overload often experienced by people with ASD.Consistency in developments (button placement, navigation, etc.) is also encouraged, making the interaction experience more predictable.The level of complexity of the instructions provided in the generated applications can be determined by the stakeholders (designers, together with family members and caregivers) in the early stages of application design, thus being able to adjust it to the developmental level of the user with ASD.

With this collective, special attention must be paid to sensory issues.Some users may be hypersensitive or hyposensitive to sensory stimuli (visual, auditory, tactile) [2].The software should allow adjustment of sensory stimuli (e.g., muting sounds or reducing brightness and intense contrasts).It is also necessary to reduce distractions (e.g., avoiding unnecessary animations, sudden sounds, or too bright colors that may cause distraction or sensory overload).The ability to adjust sensory features, although partially supported, is still under development in the framework.

An essential issue is the support for different communicative styles [78].As for the types of visual support provided, these should be adapted and can be based on the exclusive use of pictograms (these can be figurative or based on real pictures), as well as on the joint use of pictograms and text [103].Both modalities are supported by the MultiTEA framework.These supports would be helpful to users with ASD with limited verbal skills (usually in severity levels 2 and 3).However, users with high-functioning ASD (level 1) may prefer text-only representations.We therefore consider incorporating this possibility in future work as well.

To support diversity, it is also necessary to consider accessibility issues [104].Therefore, it is proposed to incorporate a series of additional features and functionalities, for which the main guidelines and recommendations that have addressed the accessibility of applications oriented to ASD users will be reviewed [63,105,106].The cross-platform approach of the framework already favors accessibility, as well as support for the comorbidity present in some users with ASD.Thus, for example, tactile interfaces will be easier to use for those who also have limited motor skills.Among the accessibility features and functionalities to be included, support for redundant and multimedia representations is currently being worked on, such as the inclusion of text-to-speech (TTS) functionality, for which pictogram description attributes are already available in the design and codesign phases.Time management functionalities are also being incorporated into transitions, activities, and feedback.In addition, other customization and accessibility features are being incorporated, such as the possibility to disable or adjust the level and intensity of sounds, modify the color palette and contrast, incorporate the dark color mode, and modify the font type and size.It is also necessary to provide the possibility to modify the layout and size of the on-screen controls to assist users with motor difficulties.To support all these additional features, the framework will allow, in the customization phase (stage 2), the activation of these accessibility features, which will become available in the final user interface (stage 3), so that users and tutors can activate or customize these aspects quickly, easily, and effortlessly.

It is also proposed to include timers, numbered steps (when using visual sequences), as well as the possibility of "pausing" a task if it is overwhelming for the user.These functionalities will improve the structuring of the tasks to be performed as well as aspects related to emotional regulation.

Another proposal to be included in the MultiTEA framework is the improvement and extension of the set of activities supported.To this end, it is proposed to make available a repository of predefined activity templates, created with the assistance of ASD experts, from which family members and therapists only have to personalize and adapt for specific ASD users.The use of these templates would allow going directly to stage 2 of the described process in cases where it is deemed necessary, as proposed by some of the participants in the preliminary evaluation.

As a previous step to the creation of this repository of activities, it is necessary to identify and specify the types of activities that could be supported by the framework.As described previously, the current version of the framework supports planning and emotion recognition activities, but the creation of an exhaustive activity taxonomy to be supported is planned.Taking as a starting point works that have already tried to classify or categorize the type of activities oriented to train the social and communicative skills of people with ASD [68], it is proposed to support the following set of activities:

-Augmentative and alternative communication notebooks.They constitute the basic communication tool for ASD users, mainly non-verbal.At the moment, we are working on the generation of AAC notebooks with vocabularies limited to specific domains (e.g., medical or school contexts).However, we are working on the possibility of incorporating pictograms into the notebook through a search engine and making use of the API provided by the ARASACC 11 association for the importation of pictograms.-Option matching and classification activities.This type of activity is already supported in the framework.Although Table 1 has shown its instantiation in the domain of emotion recognition, this type of activity is generalizable to classification and option mapping activities in other domains.Whenever there is a target category and a set of items to be classified or response options, matching and classification activities could be modeled using the current version of the framework.Therefore, this type of activity is considered technologically supported, and it is merely the responsibility of the activity designer to correctly choose the images that constitute the target and the options.-Pairing activities.This type of activity is a generalization of the previous one, in which there are several target options and various response options, with only one valid pairing between each target-option pair.-Sequence reordering activities.Another type of activity, often used for learning and training routines, are activities of reordering sequences of steps (represented by images or pictograms).This type of activity would be an evolution of the supported planning activity, in which node reordering (i.e., a redefinition of the links between nodes) is allowed.

Further work will be done to identify more types of activities, but most of the applications analyzed for working on and training communication and socialization skills fall into one of the categories listed above.

In addition, the ability to adapt and customize activities supported by this framework will allow training and practice of a wide range of day-to-day activities that involve planning (e.g., attending a medical appointment, going to school, shopping at the supermarket), communication (in clinical contexts, at work, in the classroom), as well as the social interactions needed in these contexts.

Finally, it is also proposed to improve the collaboration mechanisms, specifically, to support communication in the co-design stage.To this end, additional video and audio channels will be incorporated.

As this section has highlighted, there is still work to be done to enhance and extend the MultiTEA framework in order to effectively and efficiently support the widest possible range of users with ASD.
Limitations and challenges

Although the evaluation carried out has yielded promising results, it should be noted that qualitative and subjective surveys, such as the one used, may provide biased responses since the results are based on the respondents' perceptions.On the other hand, although the measuring instrument used is based on validated surveys, future work is planned to expand the items that make up the questionnaire and check its reliability and validity.Furthermore, the results obtained should be considered with caution and not representative of the population of target users of the MultiTEA framework since only a relatively small sample of subjects and only one of the roles involved in the supported process (ASD experts) participated in it.Therefore, a more complete evaluation of the framework and the tools generated to evaluate the usefulness, usability, and effectiveness of the products obtained by applying this framework is needed.

Although a preliminary evaluation has been carried out with experts and therapists, which has served to obtain a first impression of the usefulness and acceptance of the framework, it is necessary to rely on the assessment of the rest of the end-users: the ASD users and their families.Their insights and feedback will be essential in refining the framework and ensuring that it truly meets the needs of the end-users [107].

To ensure effective implementation of technologies in clinical practice, there is a need for more extensive experimentation over longer follow-up periods, as well as research into user acceptability, and the economic impact and clinical effectiveness of the use of this technology in healthcare environments.This type of evaluation continues to be a challenge in most studies addressing this issue [108].With the aim of addressing a more complete evaluation of the MultiTEA framework in the future, the use of specific techniques [66] and methodologies [64] for the evaluation of software aimed at the group of ASD users is proposed.

Another challenge for the transfer of the described framework, as pointed out by some of the participants in the preliminary evaluation, is the possible lack of training or skills in new technologies for some of the roles involved in the supported process.The lack of digital competencies among the potential users of MultiTEA may be a limitation for its use and a risk factor for its adoption [109].In any case, we are working on the creation of tutorials and step-by-step guides for the implementation and use of the tools described, both in text and audiovisual format, which will help to reduce this limitation.
Conclusions and future works

This paper describes a Model-Driven Development framework (MultiTEA) that allows the generation of single-user and collaborative applications for social skills training (anticipation and planning, and emotion recognition) by ASD users.This framework supports several stages, including participatory design phases among the main stakeholders, with the possibility that such co-design sessions can be carried out in a distributed way.The design and generation process also incorporates the validation of usability and accessibility recommendations and guidelines, which will improve the acceptance and adoption of the resulting application.

The framework presented raises a set of lines of continuation or proposals for improvement.First, we plan to support more types of activities, for which a taxonomy and characterization of types of activities oriented to this user collective will be created from an exhaustive analysis of existing applications.It is also deemed necessary to provide the possibility of restarting the activities as well as incorporate progress and end indicators.It is also helpful to embed multimedia resources (such as videos) in the final application or, at least, link to them, as well as include gamification mechanisms.In any case, once it has been proven that it is technologically feasible to support all the stages of the proposed MDD development approach, its generalization, enhancement, and incorporation of additional accessibility features are planned.These improvements will enhance the framework's applicability and utility for a wider range of ASD users.

It is also planned as future work to enrich the support provided in the co-design stage (collaborative and distributed), incorporating additional video and audio channels, which will make communication between participants more effective and efficient.Once these improvements have been incorporated, more complete empirical studies to validate the framework and the tools generated will be carried out, increasing the sample size and involving the rest of the stakeholders (ASD users and their families or caregivers).

Finally, we conclude by highlighting that MultiTEA is a development framework that, compared to traditional designer-driven approaches, allows, with the participation of the main stakeholders, to obtain multiplatform applications oriented to ASD users.MultiTEA supports a participatory design process, which allows for the incorporation of several perspectives in the application design process that improves the customization of the supported activity and, therefore, the acceptance of the software product by the end-user while seeking to make it effective in terms of therapeutic objectives.The distinctive and original contribution of this work lies in the proposal of a method for designing and automatically generating cross-platform applications using a model-driven approach.Although there are existing works that focus on designing systems for this user group (Section 2.2), which rely on guidelines, checklists, and methods or stages to be followed in the design process of such systems, there are no proposals that adopt the MDD approach.
We consider that this work opens up a new and promising line of research that differs from traditional development approaches and in which we plan to continue working and contributing.
